parts.title: A longer text
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I moved to Bristol for work, I hardly knew anyone. I spent most weekends at home until I noticed a community garden behind the library. Volunteers met there every Saturday to grow vegetables. I had never planted anything, but I decided to give it a try.

At first, I worried I would be useless. The other gardeners showed me how to prepare the soil and choose seeds. Soon, I was looking forward to Saturday mornings. We shared the vegetables, but the best part was getting to know people from the neighbourhood.

Six months later, I help welcome new volunteers. Last week, we planned a small café for next summer. It will use food from the garden, and local musicians have offered to play. I’m pleased the project is growing, although I hope we keep the friendly feeling that made me stay.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer first visit the garden?
options: She needed a job at the library.
She wanted to try something new.
questions.explanation: She says she had never planted anything but decided to give it a try, because she wanted something new at weekends.

questions.prompt: What was the writer worried about?
questions.explanation: She worried she would be useless, which means she was afraid she could not help.

questions.prompt: What does she say was the best part?
questions.explanation: She says the best part was getting to know people from the neighbourhood.

questions.prompt: What is planned for next summer?
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says a small café with food from the garden and local musicians is planned for next summer.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel about the project growing?
options: She thinks it is becoming too expensive.
She is happy, but wants it to stay welcoming.
She would prefer to leave the garden.
questions.explanation: She is pleased the project is growing, but hopes it keeps the friendly feeling.

parts.title: A day without a phone
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Last month, our teacher challenged the class to spend one Saturday without a mobile phone. I thought it would be easy because I rarely use mine. [1] By breakfast, I had already reached for it twice.

I put the phone in a drawer and went to meet my cousin. [2] We walked through the park and talked about our plans for the summer. Later, we visited a bookshop and found a travel guide to the coast.

At lunchtime, I wanted to check the weather. [3] Instead, the shop assistant told us that rain was expected in the afternoon. We bought two cheap umbrellas.

The rain began while we were on the bus home. [4] I noticed that I had been paying more attention to the people around me.

I still use my phone every day, but now I leave it in my bag when I am with friends. [5] The challenge was more useful than I expected.
sentences: My friends say I am better company now.
Fortunately, we were ready for it.
It felt strange to arrive without a way to tell her I was late.
But I soon discovered how much I depended on it.
I decided not to ask anyone for their phone.
My cousin has a new phone with a very good camera.

gaps.explanation: “But I soon discovered how much I depended on it” contrasts with “I thought it would be easy” and explains “reached for it twice”.
After putting the phone in the drawer and going to meet her cousin, the writer feels strange arriving without a way to tell her she was late.
“I decided not to ask anyone for their phone” follows wanting to check the weather, and “Instead” introduces what the shop assistant said.
“Fortunately, we were ready for it” links the rain with the umbrellas they had just bought.
“My friends say I am better company now” follows leaving the phone in the bag with friends and leads to the conclusion.

parts.title: The weekend project
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: My brother and I decided to [1] a small repair event at our school. We asked people to bring objects that were broken but still [2]. A local electrician kindly [3] to help us. We put up posters so that everyone would know where to [4] their things. On the day, more people came [5] we had expected. We were tired afterwards, but it was a very [6] experience.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You organise an event; the other verbs do not go with “a small repair event”.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: People brought objects that were broken but still useful, so they could be repaired.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: “Offered to help” is the correct pattern; enjoyed, finished and suggested are followed by -ing.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: People leave their things at a place; you do not borrow, throw or lose them there.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: After “more people came” a comparison needs “than”.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: “Rewarding” means giving satisfaction, which fits being tired but happy.

parts.title: A note from the coast
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Ben,
We arrived [1] the coast yesterday evening. The hotel is smaller [2] I expected, but our room has a wonderful view. We have already visited the old harbour, [3] we are going to take a boat trip tomorrow. If the weather [4] good, we’ll walk along the cliffs afterwards. I’ve never seen [5] many seabirds before! I’ll send you some photos when we get [6] home.
Love,
Mia

gaps.explanation: We say “arrive at” a place such as the coast.
“Smaller than I expected” is a comparison.
“And” adds a second plan to the one already done.
A condition in the present uses the present simple: “If the weather is good”.
“So many” goes before plural countable nouns such as seabirds.

parts.title: A talk about a nature club

turns.text: Hello, everyone. I’m Priya, and I help run the Green Steps nature club. We meet every Saturday morning at the entrance to West Park. parts.title: An interview with a young chef
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Ella, when did you first become interested in cooking?

turns.speaker: ella
turns.text: My grandmother used to let me help her make bread when I was about eight. I liked making things with my hands, but I didn’t think of it as a job then.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What did you do after school?

turns.speaker: ella
turns.text: I studied science because my parents thought it would give me more choices. I enjoyed it, but during my final year I worked in a café at weekends. That’s when I realised I wanted to cook professionally.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Was it easy to find work?

turns.speaker: ella
turns.text: Not at first. I sent my CV to several restaurants and heard nothing. A friend told me about a small hotel that needed weekend help. I learned a lot there, especially how to work quickly when the kitchen was busy.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you enjoy most now?

turns.speaker: ella
turns.text: I like creating new dishes, but seeing customers enjoy them is even better. I’m still learning every day.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What advice would you give someone starting out?

turns.speaker: ella
turns.text: Don’t worry if your first attempts go wrong. Ask questions, practise often, and be patient. I also think it’s important to learn about ingredients, not just follow recipes.

questions.explanation: Ella says her grandmother used to let her help make bread.

options: It was needed for a café job
She wanted to become a doctor
questions.explanation: She studied science because her parents thought it would give her more choices.

questions.prompt: What does Ella enjoy most about her work?
questions.explanation: She likes creating new dishes, but seeing customers enjoy them is even better.

questions.prompt: What advice does Ella give beginners?
